accuracy.evidence: States of water and rates match the Year 4 statement and BBC Bitesize KS2 'The water cycle': evaporation is liquid to gas at any temperature, faster when warmer; condensation is vapour cooling to liquid; cloud droplets are about 0.01 to 0.02 mm, given as about 0.02 mm. Saucer rates of 3, 10 and 25 ml per hour are illustrative and keep the order fridge < room < sunny sill.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the water-cycle misconceptions listed by Allen (2014) and the Nuffield SPACE evaporation report: water 'disappears' or soaks away, water must boil to evaporate, clouds or kettle steam are water vapour, and drops on a cold glass leaked or are 'sweat'. Each one has a lab step and a matching challenge distractor with its own correction.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagevap lab is new: a puddle clock with a draggable hour dial, a three-saucer temperature race, a cold-can versus warm-can wait, a ring-by-ring labelling of a sea, hill and cloud picture, and a zoom slider into a cloud whose drops join and fall. It shares no mechanic with the particles visual of lesson 101 or the separate visual of lessons 99 and 100.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step matches one learning outcome of the topic: evaporation is liquid to gas (puddle), rate of evaporation rises with temperature (saucers), condensation is gas to liquid (cold can), the four stages of the cycle in order (labelling), and clouds are liquid drops that fall as precipitation when they join (zoom). The challenge mixes all of them.

predictions.evidence: Three predict prompts come before acting: where the puddle water goes, which of the fridge, room and sunny saucers dries first, and whether a cloud is water vapour, tiny drops or smoke. Each offers the common wrong idea (soaks away, cold dries first, vapour) so the lab result directly confronts it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The seven challenge questions send wrong answers through a slip() helper with a specific fix, for example 'Boiling is fast evaporation, but puddles dry on cool days too', 'Water vapour is invisible. You can see a cloud because it is made of tiny drops or ice' and 'Glass has no holes'. The can step and the labelling step also explain each wrong pick.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and name each term once with its meaning: evaporation, water vapour, condensation, precipitation, collection. The adult text quotes the Year 4 statement, separates boiling from evaporation, and lists the slips to listen for. Both passed the family readability targets in validate_lessons.

no_filler.evidence: There is no stock opener or summary line. Every kid paragraph holds one everyday example (a puddle, a hot day, a cold can, the sea and rain) and every adult paragraph a standard, a rule, a misconception list or a description of the lab. The content gate's filler and overlap checks passed.

mobile.evidence: Phone screenshots in light and dark at 390 px show the puddle, saucers, cans, cycle picture and cloud without overlap after moving the saucer labels above the rims and the cloud captions to the top. All actions have large buttons, and the hour and zoom dials can also be dragged with a finger.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas aria-label is updated with every spoken message, buttons all have text, saucer buttons carry labels like 'Sunny sill saucer', feedback uses a polite live region, and axe reported no violations in either theme. Drops on the cold can were made light in dark mode so they stay visible against the blue can.
